question: For centuries, inland fishing, aquaculture and angling have helped guarantee food security and create ecologically valuable cultural landscapes. Over the last decade, however, the EU’s level of self-sufficiency when it comes to fishery products has fallen from around 50 % to 30 %, while its reliance on imports has increased.

Despite the significant benefits that inland fishing brings to the environment and tourism, and the role it plays in feeding the population, the sector has been struggling economically and traditional angling practices are at risk of disappearing. The situation is heavily influenced by catch results and price and cost trends. More important still is the fact that catches have dropped in many areas.

Further to the environmental changes occurring in waters, predators like cormorants and otters are also to blame. On top of this, fish losses caused by power plants not only pose a threat to biodiversity but to the economic capacity of the inland fishing sector. These developments make angling less attractive and lay its preservation as part of our cultural heritage on the line. 1.
Are there plans to update EU legislation on cormorants, for example, to also take into account the economic interests of inland fishing alongside nature conservation?
In view of the months-long ban on eel fishing, how will the Commission strike a balance between the interests of nature conservation and those of inland fishing?
To ensure sustainable water management is successfully implemented, will it take greater heed of anglers’ expertise in aquatic ecosystems when making decisions?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.10.2024) While there is no specific EU legislation on cormorants, they are protected1 under the Birds Directive2. The Commission is aware that a recent expansion of the cormorant population can make the balancing of conflicts between human interests and cormorants challenging.

The Commission has published advice on managing such conflicts3, and points to the possibility to use derogations under Article 9 of the Birds Directive. Guidance on applying such derogations is under development. The current eel fishing closure established by the EU applies only to inland waters in the Mediterranean region4.

This six-month ban stems from Recommendation GFCM/42/2018/15 of the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean6, extended by Recommendations GFCM/45/2022/17 and GFCM/46/2023/18, and most recently implemented into EU law through Regulation (EU) 2024/2599. The Water Framework Directive (WFD)10 provides for the management of surface and groundwaters to ensure the good status of all waters.

Article 14 requires Member States to ensure that all interested parties are actively involved in the implementation of the Directive, and that all draft planning documents are consulted publicly. This allows anglers and stakeholders11 to contribute, e.g. on characterising and classifying water bodies, identifying pressures, and setting mitigation and restoration measures.

The European Anglers Alliance is an active stakeholder in the Common Implementation Strategy for the WFD. Additionally, under the Common Fisheries Policy12, fisheries associations are members in Advisory Councils, which advice on conservation and socio-economic aspects of management, as well as on simplification of rules.
